utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 16th of February, 2011. Good morning to the accused, to the Defence counsel, and the OTP representatives, and all the people assisting us. Ms. Nozica is going to proceed without further ado in her closing arguments for Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Your Honours, yesterday, in the first part of our closing argument, we spoke about the impressions that the representatives of international organisations shared before this Trial Chamber or in their report, and those impressions regarded Bruno Stojic. We saw exactly what kind of impressions those were, and I suppose that the Trial Chamber will wonder how come the several representatives of international organisations acquired similar impressions and opinions about Bruno Stojic. Your Honours, Bruno Stojic's Defence claims that that opinion and that perception was actually created by Bo Pellnas, who organised a meeting on the 17th of April, 1993, in Mostar. You will remember the meeting, certainly. That was the meeting to which Bo Pellnas brought a member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Ganic. Bruno Stojic did enter the room where the meeting was being held, and he said that the BiH Army in Central Bosnia had launched attacks against the HVO. Obviously, Bo Pellnas was not happy about that. He was actually very angry because he was the only that who provided details in his own report, and those details are not conveyed by any other reports from that same meeting. In front of the door of the room where the meeting was held, and not in the room where the meeting was held, Witness Beese was standing, and it was obvious that Bo Pellnas and Beese jointly created a position about Bruno Stojic and conveyed it onto other people. The Trial Chamber heard the testimonies of international monitors, and they heard that they moved around the vast area and that they had contacts with a large number of people. For that reason, and also because they didn't have time to be briefed prior to their arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had to rely on information provided to them by others, by other fellow monitors, and they never bothered to double-check that information. Many of them had preconceived notions when they arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as we heard in the testimony of Witness Slobodan Bozic, who was a member of the HVO HZ-HB commission for relations with international monitors, and he had most contacts with international monitors. This is referred to in paragraph P30 of the Prosecutor's final brief. Again in this paragraph, the Prosecutor refers to Witness Beese. The paragraph number is 530. Judge Prandler is warning me to be even slower than I have been so far. There were a lot of reports about this meeting. Only in the collective report drafted by Bo Pellnas which was drafted on the 23rd of April as a summary of all the other reports, and that was six days after the meeting, there is a statement to the effect that Stojic had threatened, that he had insulted Ganic, and that he had a pistol on his body. That is document P2024 -- 54, 2054. These allegations are not corroborated by any other reports from that same meeting. Not even the testimonies by participants in the meeting, Mr. Petkovic, Witness 1DAA, and (redacted). The reports that describe the meeting and that do not corroborate allegations proffered by Bo Pellnas are the following, and I would like to draw your attention to the fact that those are ECMM reports, and I would also like to remind you that Witness Beese was one of the monitors of that same organisation. The documents in question are P1950, P1965, P1980, and finally, P2016. All of the aforementioned reports describe the situation in an identical way. They all say that Bruno Stojic entered the room where the meeting was being held and that he said that the BiH Army had launched a large-scale offensive in Central Bosnia, and then the meeting was adjourned. I would like to remind the Honourable Chamber that in these reports it is stated that up to then all the key decisions had already been made about the establishment of commissions which would be in charge of relieving tensions in Mostar. These reports do not say anything either about an alleged attack on Ganic or threats, nor does anybody mention the fact that Bruno Stojic might have had a pistol. It arises from the testimony of Milivoj Petkovic, as recorded on pages 50068 through 50071, that the meeting was almost over when Bruno Stojic arrived with a report on an ABiH attack in Travnik. Bruno Stojic did not attack a person. He did not insult anybody. He did not have a pistol, because Witness Petkovic never saw Mr. Bruno Stojic carrying a pistol. Mr. Petkovic, furthermore, said that Ganic remained in Mostar on the following day, on the 19th of April, 1993, and that on the 20th of April, 1993, they travelled together to Zenica, escorted by UNPROFOR, because there was a meeting to be held in Zenica. Your Honours, I am providing all these details, because Mr. Bo Pellnas, when he testified before this Trial Chamber, told us a very dramatic story and describe a dramatic situation. Allegedly after Mr. Ganic had been threatened, they had to escort them. However, we can see from Mr. Petkovic's testimony that the situation was quite normal, that the two of them went to that meeting in a very normal way, and that Mr. Ganic had stayed on in Mostar for two days after the meeting. Witness 1DAA described Mr. Bruno Stojic's behaviour in an identical manner, and that was recorded on pages 28905 through 29002. Your Honours, the minutes of the session of the HVO HZ-HB, dated 19 April 1993, confirms that -- the information about the ABiH attack against the HVO. That means that that session took place one day after the meeting with Ganic, and this is reported in document 1D1664. At that session, the follow thing was discussed, and I quote: "The dramatic reports which have been arriving from Zenica, Vitez, and Busovaca over the past few days." Those dramatic reports were not conveyed at that session by Mr. Bruno Stojic, because he never attended that session. And while Mr. Ganic, a member of the BiH Presidency and a member of the Supreme Command of the BH Army was in Mostar on the 19th of April, 1993, a very well-known order was drafted by the 4th Corps, an order which was admitted into evidence under P1970. That order represented a plan of attack by the BiH Army on the HVO in Mostar, and that attack was ultimately carried out on the 9th of May, 1993. This is fully corroborated by an excerpt from the book "Bosniak Croatian Political Showdown," authored by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic on page 197 which has been admitted into evidence under 3D3101. So when we follow the planned course of attack as described in the aforementioned order, and when we look at the description of events in the aforementioned books -- book provided by Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic who, at the time, was the president of the SDA for the city of Mostar, we can conclude that the attack was carried out pursuant to the ordered -- order issued on the 19th of April, 1993. I understand that one number has not been recorded. I'm not able to follow. It is possible that P1970 was not recorded, but we have an agreement that after the session we are going to check the transcript and compare it with the verbal arguments. We don't have to waste any time on that at the moment. Your Honours, it is very difficult to believe that Mr. Ganic, as vice-president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and more importantly as a member of the Supreme Command of the BiH Army, did not take an active part in taking a decision to issue that order, and all that at the time when he attended the meeting with HVO representatives and advocated peace. This was sure duplicity and a double game played on his part. The Prosecutor furthermore describes Bruno Stojic as a hard-liner. In footnote 1214, the Prosecutor refers to paragraph 62 in the statement of Witness BA, which has been admitted into evidence under P9712. Your Honour, we claim that no such position was ever presented in that footnote. However, this part of the statement is very important for a different reason. Since the document is under seal, I'm going to read just one little part:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, and I apologise to my colleague and I'm sorry to be violating, I guess, the code of silence, but there has been a statement that shouldn't have been made on the record, and I want to draw -- if we could go to private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I apologise. I will then kindly ask the Court to move into private session and then I'll repeat the important parts of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to remind you once again that that happened on the 10th of June, 1993, and I will also remind you of a document, P2690, which was a communique signed by Bruno Stojic after the attack in Travnik. As we read this statement provided by a Prosecution witness, we can see that indeed there had been an attack in Travnik prior to the 9th of June, 1993. We have already spoken about that in paragraph 528. However, Your Honours, what matters and what needs to be emphasised here is the fact that the HVO did not respond to those attacks because already on the 12th of June, 1993, an agreement was signed about the end of hostilities between the BiH Army. The document number is P2726. Yet the BiH Army continued its offensive in Central Bosnia, which is also confirmed by an UNPROFOR report under P2750. Your Honours, we have presented a large number of documents which confirm this fact. However, on this occasion, I wanted to present an objective report, as it were, the report by UNPROFOR, which is very important because it is a day-to-day account of what was going on in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I think we should avoid reference to reports by a society, an institution which is so touchy about secrecy. They are not -- the public is not supposed to know that we have as evidence reports of this organisation. I think we should redact that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, UNPROFOR reports do not fall under that category. I may have been misunderstood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I may also be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this part of our final argument, we were dealing with some of the reports provided by international organisations which contained opinions and conclusions which were not founded on the events on the ground. Thank you, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. You know, we said nobody's perfect. Everybody makes mistakes. Your Honours, we have demonstrated that some assessments and perceptions of people and the entire HZ-HB were subjective and biased. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas also spoke about that. The Honourable Honours could also hear that when those witnesses were -- provided their testimonies. I am convinced that that was also sometimes your own perception. We all remember Witness BH who provided his assessments about the situation in Mostar. When my learned friend Mrs. Alaburic asked him where the Vranica building was he didn't know. He could not answer. He also didn't know what had happened on the 9th of May, 1993. His Honour Judge Antonetti expressed his surprise when he realised that this witness was not that familiar with the situation in Mostar, and you will find that on transcript pages 17714 and 17715. That person was a high-ranking international official. Nevertheless, they still drafted reports and sent it to their superiors irrespective of the fact that they did not have reliable and complete information. Your Honours, all Resolutions by the Security Council relied on the reports of the international monitors who were on the ground, who were in the area. We have seen in this courtroom, at least partly, at least to a certain extent, how those reports were drafted, and based on those reports, the indictment was issued against these six accused, including my client, for a joint criminal enterprise. These reports represented just tiny pieces from which a big mosaic was created that finally led to the signing of peace agreements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Dayton Constitution -- or, rather, the Dayton Accords were signed under the auspices of the international community, and the international community relied on reports from the area and rewarded the campaign of ethnical cleansing in Republika Srpska and recognised that area as a separate entity. Before this Trial Chamber and before this Court, which was established by one and the same Security Council, many convictions were brought for genocide and other gravest and most heinous crimes against the political and military representatives of Republika Srpska. At the same time, this Prosecutor's office, as a part of the international court, proclaimed the HZ-HB a para-state, and the Prosecutor repeated that in his final argument. So it was based on the Dayton Accord that a state was created, which even today, 15 years after that Accord, cannot seem to function, but that is hardly surprising. There are two entities, of which one has the attributes of a state, even a flag, a hymn, or a national anthem, actually, and the other is divided into ten cantons. There are 13 governments, and the state is headed by three presidents. The majority of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, even today, think that the organisational structure imposed by the Dayton Accord has prevented them from realising their rights as one of the constituent people. Even in countries with developed democracies, it is always the least numerous people that is faced with the greatest problems, and that is especially true in a state structured such as this. These unresolved relations between the peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina have brought Bosnia-Herzegovina to a deadlock, especially these days when the representatives of the Croats and BiH again advocate the restructuring of Bosnia-Herzegovina to realise their rights as a constituent people. The official authorities in Zagreb also voice their concern for the position of the Croats in BiH, although President Tudjman died long ago. This is also advocated by the president of Croatia, who is a social democrat, and also by the prime minister who belongs to the HDZ, and other leading politicians who, at Franjo Tudjman's times, were in the opposition. A third entity in the Herceg-Bosna are no longer a taboo as was the case after the war and all the way until the October elections in 2010. We have heard witnesses here who were replaced from their positions by the High Representative in BiH, who was actually the highest authority there, and they were replaced when -- because they spoke about a third entity, or call it Herceg-Bosna. Nowadays, these are no longer taboos, and nowadays the High Representative no longer takes the measures that he used to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we've been giving broad latitude, this is far afield and I don't believe it's in evidence in record. The evidence has to be -- what is submitted to the Court has to be in evidence in record. Now talking about what happened in the last couple of weeks is not in evidence, should not be referred to, and it is also inaccurate. It was just several days ago that the United States ambassador to Bosnia condemned a continuing effort to create a third entity in Bosnia. The United States ambassador came out and said, We reject the creation of a third entity, a Croat entity, et cetera, et cetera. So number one, it's not in evidence. It should not be included; number two, it's wrong. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do, with regret, deprecate this intervention. I do deprecate it. It is a matter of very well-known professional courtesy that closing speeches are not interrupted. We gave the Prosecution that courtesy. And we didn't agree with a lot of what they said, whether it was grandchildren or thugs or invective. We kept quiet. Your Honours, if inaccuracies are said, Mr. Scott, on behalf of the Prosecutor, can make an application at the end to rise and address them, but I would ask that he be restrained and remain seated -- and remain seated and allow this final speech and the voice of Mr. Stojic to be heard and not drowned out by interruptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. Excuse me, Your Honours. Let me respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is that I come from a system where the voice of the Prosecution and the voice of the Defence is never interrupted by the other party. I was a Prosecutor and it never occurred that anyone interrupted my closing arguments, and I never saw the opposite either. I will now consult with my colleagues to see what should be done. I believe that what has happened is quite extraordinary, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want to add, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I rose to my feet with great reservation and the Chamber fully knows that I have sat here for the last two-plus days and not gotten up to my feet. I'm happy to sit here and take insults to myself, insults to Prosecutor counsel, and that we've been sleazy and unethical. They can attack me all they want. But what is put before the Chamber and argued does have to be in evidence. It has to be in evidence. And that's the difference in terms of factual assertions. Now, this is not argument. These are factual assertions being made. It is only become an extreme basis that I rose to my feet. I apologise to that, but I think this is completely different than broad latitude in arguing inferences. This is an -- inferences. These are factual assertions about things that are not in evidence. Excuse me, and I apologise if I offended the Chamber. I did so with great reluctance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated, as you see, and would like to remind you that there was a written decision from the Chamber in which it said that there should be no objection from any party, from any party, I repeat, Prosecution or Defence, when the other party was making its closing arguments. So we anticipated the problem, and therefore we dismiss Mr. Scott's objection regarding the words spoken by Mr. Stojic's Defence. Mrs. Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add one thing. The Trial Chamber also reminds everyone that the Prosecutor, after closing arguments, can -- can request to have the floor as rebuttal, and the Trial Chamber will allow this or not, but this -- what you said, Mr. Scott, could have been said after the closing arguments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm very glad that Mr. Scott intervened, because I said nothing else but that this is something that's discussed publicly today in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that a third entity or another solution today is a topic dealt with by many political factors in the world who have understood that both Herzegovina, as it was created by the Dayton Accord, cannot function. I am familiar with the position of the American ambassador who opposes the creation of a third entity. That's true. But it's also true that it's a topic of discussion which we -- which I have said. For a long time, that wasn't the case, and the very fact that this is being discussed, whether anybody agrees or disagrees with it, now after 15 years is significant in itself. We would like to point out that these six accused were in no position to exert influence on such demands put forward by the BiH Croats, because they have been in detention for five years. I have put this matter forward, because the Trial Chamber will take its decision about the joint criminal enterprise based on the facts in the case file and based on the generally known facts of the present time, because two things are going done in parallel, this trial and repeated criticism on the part of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina due to their inability to realise their constitutional rights. That is relevant for a number of allegations put forward by the Prosecution with regard to the JCE in their final arguments. Now I'd like to discuss the allegation that Bruno Stojic consciously and significantly contributed to the JCE of Herceg-Bosna. In paragraph 532, the Prosecution strived to show the participation of Bruno Stojic in the JCE since 1991 when he was assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by virtue of this function, he was also a member of the Crisis Staff of the HDZ. This allegation of the Prosecution, namely that Bruno Stojic as member of the HDZ Crisis Staff, actually began his activity as part of the JCE cannot stand its ground. Bruno Stojic, acting as assistant minister of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by virtue of his position was a member of the HDZ Crisis Staff. This was confirmed by Prosecution witness Stjepan Kljuic. The transcript page is 7962 through 7966. That body was neither illegal nor criminal. It was headed by Stjepan Kljuic, a moderate Croat, as he has been called several times by the Prosecution. It was a task of the HDZ Crisis Staff to protect citizens, because it was obvious that the defence system in Bosnia-Herzegovina had collapsed. It was based, first and foremost, on the JNA. Bruno Stojic was assistant minister of the interior of the Republic of BiH, in charge of finance. At that time, after the first multi-party elections, the minister was a Muslim. The ministry adopted decisions at the collegium of ministers, and Bruno Stojic went about his tasks professionally and in accordance with the laws and regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina, advocating an integral whole Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is especially corroborated by document 2D841. This is the content of testimony of Witness Davor Korac, who at the time worked at that ministry. The transcript reference is 38825 through 38832. Bruno Stojic didn't leave Sarajevo to join the HZ-HB. Bruno Stojic at that time lived in Neum with his family, and he went there every weekend to see his family. In early April 1992, while he was in Neum, all points of entry to Sarajevo were blocked, and Bruno Stojic was unable to return to his job. Witness Davor Korac says as much on transcript pages 38825 through 38826. Furthermore, it is correct, as put forward by the Prosecution, that Bruno Stojic participated in the procurement of weapons in that period because that was part of his job as assistant minister of the interior, but these weapons were distributed to both Croats and Muslims. Witness Zoran Buntic -- Witness Zoran Buntic confirms that on transcript pages 30587 through 30592, and Witness Slobodan Bozic on transcript pages 36192 through 36196. There's also another document to corroborate this, and that's an excerpt from Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic's book, who, as I said, at the time was the president of the SDA for the city of Mostar, and his book is Exhibit 2D976. Apart from that, there is also the testimony of Hamid Bahto on transcript pages 37900 and the following, and there's also a document -- or, rather, Exhibit 2D1253. The Prosecution alleges that this Crisis Staff was -- later became the HVO army, and he cites Exhibit P56. But from the persons on the list of 13 members of the Crisis Staff of the HDZ, only one later was a member of the military component of the HVO, and that is Ivo Lozancic. In paragraph 533 and the following, Bruno Stojic's work in the Department of Defence is mentioned. We have dealt with these matters in paragraph 32 of our final brief. I would like to stress the following, though: Bruno Stojic was head of the Department of Defence from the 3rd of July, 1992, through 10 November 1993. There are -- there is evidence about the end of service of Bruno Stojic in the Department of Defence, and that is Slobodan Bozic's testimony on pages 36163 and the following, and 36204 and the following, and there's also Exhibit P6583 and Exhibit 2D416. I insist on this, Your Honours, because in the Prosecution final brief, in spite of this evidence, the Prosecution claims that Bruno Stojic remained in a leading position in the Department of Defence until late November, as if no evidence had been led before this Trial Chamber as to when exactly Bruno Stojic stood off -- stood down. We think this is very important. The Department of Defence was one of the departments of the HVO HZ-HB with the same capacity as any other department. We also refer to paragraphs 223 through 231 of the Prlic final Defence brief and the final arguments of that same Defence of 14 February 2011. Then I would like to mention that the Decree on the Armed Forces, P289 and P588, lay down the -- all relations between the bodies of the HZ-HB with the president of the HZ-HB, and that also applies to the relationship between the HVO HZ-HB and the Department of Defence. Bruno Stojic reported to the HVO HZ-HB for his work there, as all other heads of departments, and, in his work he had no direct link with the president HZ-HB, either de jure or de facto. The relationship between the Department of Defence and the president of the HZ-HB was purely of administrative nature and had to do with appointing officers at lower positions in the military component of the HVO. But let us return to the position of the Department of Defence of the HVO HZ-HB. The Department of Defence compiled a programme of work based on requests issued by the HVO HZ-HB, as all other departments, which is corroborated by Exhibit 1D110, Exhibit P4890, and P646. The Department of Defence submitted reports on its work to the HVO HZ-HB as all other departments did. The HVO HZ-HB forwarded this report to the president of the HZ-HB. The Main Staff, separately from the Department of Defence, also submitted its own report to the HVO HZ-HB, and that was forwarded to the president. This is confirmed by Exhibits P128 and P4699. I deliberately ignore documents created after 10 November 1992 when Bruno Stojic was no longer head of the Department of Defence. These reports were accepted by the -- or approved by the HVO HZ-HB, which is corroborated by Exhibit 1D1607 and P4008. The Department of Defence made proposals for the appointment of officials to be appointed by the HVO HZ-HB as any other department did, and the Department of Defence received funds for its work and the military component of the HVO, because the HVO HZ-HB in 1992 and 1993, as all other departments, didn't -- didn't have its own budget. I will mention the relevant documents: P578, P950, P1137, P1197, P1324, P1388, P -- excuse me 1D1183, P5799, and, finally, P6689. This is a letter of the government of the HR HB dated 16 December 1993, which was sent to all municipalities. From it we can see that the government, based on the decisions of the Assembly, requests the establishment of a single financial system to fund the defence, the police, and the judiciary, which shows that even as -- in late 1993, this financial system at the level of the HZ-HB had not been established, which -- which confirms the allegations of Defence in their final briefs that the municipalities actually played the main role in the funding of the army. The head of the Department of Defence informed the HVO HZ-HB generally about the security situation, but the HVO HZ-HB also invited the leading persons from the Main Staff to meetings when it wanted precise information. The relevant documents have already been mentioned. Matters from the remit of the Department of Defence have been discussed at almost 80 per cent of the meetings of the HVO HZ-HB. We have no time to list them all but believe that these, as all other documents, too, will certainly be carefully scrutinised by the Trial Chamber. Although most meetings dealt with Defence matters, at no one meeting was a discussion about operative commanding -- commanding the HVO, because that wasn't part of the remit of the Department of Defence or that of the HVO HZ-HB. So if we look at the minutes from all meetings of the HVO HZ-HB, we see that the Department of Defence, as all other departments, depended on the decisions taken by the HVO HZ-HB and had no specific positions, nor did it have any special links with Boban that would affect its work. Jadranko Prlic's Defence tried to suggest to the Trial Chamber that the Department of Defence had special links with the president of the HZ-HB, which simply -- which is simply wrong. Bruno Stojic didn't issue declarations with Mate Boban, but Jadranko Prlic did, which is logical with regard to his position. Document P2346 corroborates that, and we see what the military situation was like there. Although the Prlic Defence tries to push out the Department of Defence from the HVO HZ-HB, they cannot achieve that, because the evidence points to the contrary, and so does common sense. It's the Decree on the Armed Forces, P289 and P58, is the basic legislative document that determines the remit of the Department of Defence and its head. The -- there's also the decision on the basic structure of the Department of Defence, which is P586, and there's the decision on the organisation and the responsibility of the departments and commissions of the HVO HZ-HB, which is P440. It follows from all these that the Department of Defence, with regard to the H -- the military component of the HVO, is in charge of administrative and professional matters as well as budget and material supply. The head of the Department of Defence did not command the army. That remit was -- that was the Main Staff's remit. We have spoke about that in detail in paragraph 331 of our final brief. We will briefly dwell only on document P586 to explain the remit of the head of Bruno Stojic with regard to the brigade commanders. This is a reply to paragraphs 6510 -- 65 through 106 and 376 through 364 and 614 of the Petkovic Defence brief, final brief. Now, with regard to the paragraph I mentioned in the Petkovic final brief, we would like to stress that the brigade commanders were not subordinate to the head of defence except in matters outlined in Article 9. There's no one -- there's no evidence that brigade commanders turned to Bruno Stojic with regard to matters that were not mentioned in Article 9. With regard to the aforementioned paragraphs in the Petkovic Defence final brief, I would like to say that brigade commanders were not subordinated to the head of the Defence Department, with the only exception being financial matters and budgetary issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer have any interpretation into French. It's back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. There is no single piece of evidence corroborating the fact that brigade commanders were subordinated to Bruno Stojic with regard to any activities or tasks, with the only exception being financial matters, administrative matters, budgetary matters, and organisational issues. There's no single piece of evidence that brigade commanders addressed Bruno Stojic and brought before him any other issues but the aforementioned ones. There's no single piece of evidence that Bruno Stojic issued a single order to brigade commanders, with the only exception being those that dealt with administrative issues. And finally, it arises from the Petkovic final brief that the head of Defence Department was superior to the brigade commanders with regard to the operation of prison because -- of prisons because this was a non-combat activity. This is not corroborated by a single piece of evidence. In footnote 646 of Petkovic's final brief, allegedly there is evidence which corroborate this thesis and those are reports of the SIS of the brigades and not brigade commanders. In paragraph 332 of our final brief, we provided relevant evidence as to how the SIS functioned in the area -- area of HZ-HB and proof which demonstrated without any doubt that assistance for SIS in the brigades were subordinated to the brigade commanders. This was confirmed by Zrinko Tokic, who testified on behalf of both Praljak and Petkovic, and his testimony was recorded on pages T45458, lines 10 to 5. Tokic then alleges that Bruno Stojic remained active in the area of arms and logistics as the head of department for production and sale of weapons and military equipment of the HR HB upon assuming those duties and tasks on the 16th of December, 1993. The Prosecutor did not provide any evidence to this Trial Chamber about the role of Bruno Stojic in the JCE after his departure from the position as the head of the Defence Department on the 10th of November, 1993. Bruno Stojic's Defence claims, with regard to paragraph 339 which deals with the ultimatum story, that there was no ultimatum on the 15th of January, 1993. There was none in mid-April 1993. A lot of detail to that effect have been provided in paragraphs 243 of our final brief. With regard to the authorities of Bruno Stojic to issue the order which was admitted into evidence under P1140, this is the order dated 15 January 1993, which is portrayed as an ultimatum. We would like to point out that he only implemented a decision of the HVO HZ-HB in keeping with his authorities pursuant to Article 9 on the decision of the organisation of the Defence Department. And here we would like to point out that the order issued by Bruno Stojic shows that this could not be an ultimatum. And the same applies to the order issued by General Petkovic. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to pay particular attention to Article 1 in Bruno Stojic's order where it says that the Main Staff of the armed forces of the HVO must establish contact with all operation zone and staffs of the BH Army in the territories of provinces 3, 8, 10, 1, 5 and 9, with a view to finalising details of the implementation of this decision of the HVO HZ-HB. That decision was admitted into evidence and clearly shows that that could not have been an ultimatum, given the fact that contact had to be established with commanders and staffs in the territories of various provinces as mentioned in that order. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to reconsider and carefully analyse all of those documents that deal with the alleged ultimatum. For the long five years, those documents have been referred to as an ultimatum, so it should be very careful in evaluating whether they, indeed, were an ultimatum, because where I come from, there is a notorious truth which says if you repeat a lie ample times, it becomes true, true, and that applies to this alleged ultimatum. It was not an ultimatum, and I'm sure that the Honourable Chamber will be able to realise very quickly what this was all about. In document 1139, bullet point 7, it says: "Commanders of operative zones are hereby tasked with establishing contacts with the commands of the BiH and find the best solutions for establishing joint commands." This is General Petkovic's orders. How can these decisions be ultimatum but they can only be realised in co-operation with the ABiH? These documents were drafted based on the agreed positions of the negotiators -- negotiators in Geneva and the talks between Izetbegovic and Boban in Zagreb, as General Praljak testified before this Trial Chamber on pages 40568 through 40573 and confirmed by Witness Bozo Rajic. When these documents were issued and when we heard the testimony of Mr. Praljak, this was corroborated by the testimony of Mr. Bozo Rajic, who, at the time, was Defence minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who testified before this Court and his testimony -- his statement was admitted at 2D1409. In the order issued by the minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who also included into his order the units of the Army of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, Article 6, states that the implementation of the order will be the duty of Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO; Colonel Sefer Halilovic; and Colonel Ratko Mladic. The order was issued on the 21st January 1993. The document number is 2D441, and the deadline for the implementation of the order or for its execution is the end of negotiations in Geneva. Why were there objections to the order being carried out and why Mr. Izetbegovic changed his position? It suffices to look at document 2D48 which the Trial Chamber members have in their binders and this is an interview given by Sefer Halilovic to El Pais on the 27th of January, 1993. In that interview, he said that nobody could destroy the idea of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a single integral and sovereign state through no negotiations. He said negotiations are all well and good, but if a different result is achieved, we will prevail in a battlefield. And then there is a journalist -- the journalist's comment, and he says Halilovic's opinion probably has more weight than the opinion of President Izetbegovic, although Halilovic does not have his chair at roundtable in Geneva. He is still the one who represents those who fight on the front lines. And finally let me say that there was no ultimatum. This was just an attempt to organise Bosnia-Herzegovina in the way that was agreed -- agreed by the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Geneva. However, the government in Sarajevo withdrew their consent after decisions and orders had been issued by the HVO HZ-HB. Since the Prosecutor shows this ultimatum as one of the most important pieces of evidence corroborated -- corroborating the existence of the JCE, we have to ask ourselves what would have happened if those decisions had been implemented jointly and in co-operation? One of the very significant options is this: There would have never been a war between Bosniaks and Croats, because everything would have been resolved in January 1991. The problem between Bosniaks, who were then known as Muslims and Croats, from the very outset was different ideas of the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is precisely what General Halilovic talks about in his interview. On the one hand, there was a desire of the government in Sarajevo for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be organised as an integral state; and, on the other hand, there was a desire of a majority of the Croatian people to decentralise the state and break it down into -- into either cantons or provinces or an association of republics. The concept was accepted by the international community. So the concept of the internal reorganisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they offered different solutions which were all to the last accepted by the representatives of the HZ-HB. However, none of those solutions were adopted or approved by the government in Sarajevo. Under the pressure of the international community, the war was ended, and the Washington Agreement was signed. The Washington agreement follows the demands of the representatives of the HZ-HB, because the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been split into cantons. It has been divided into cantons. In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as we could see in Exhibits 2D1183, Article 1, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO have been recognised as the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and nothing has changed to this day. Deadlines were given to establish a Joint Command, and that was done, but that was done only two years after the war and after the collapse of the concept of a unitarian or a single state that was advocated by Alija Izetbegovic from the beginning of the attempts to organise Bosnia-Herzegovina. Just like my learned friend Mr. Ken Scott did it, I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to carefully read the transcript from the meeting between Presidents Izetbegovic and Tudjman, dated 12 July 1992. The document number is P336. This transcript shows that there was a conflict between those two concepts of the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The concept of a unitarian state, on the one hand, and the concept of a state divided into cantons on the other. All of this certainly has to be put into the perspective of solutions as proffered by the Washington Agreement. This transcript clearly shows, and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic confirmed that, that the HVO was the first to organise themselves for the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time when the government forces did not exist and were not organised. This transcript shows that Mr. Izetbegovic is grateful to -- to Croatia for everything that they had done for the refugees up to then. The transcript also shows that Alija Izetbegovic wanted Croatia to continue assisting Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also it shows his reluctance to accept Croatian demands for the cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm now moving on to paragraph 540, and I'm following my own thesis about the way the decision was made on the 15th of January, 1993, the same decision that the Prosecutor calls an ultimatum. He wants to transfer that same picture and image on to the events which took place after the 30th of June, 1993, and again, he's referring to Exhibits P3038, and that's the proclamation which signed jointly by Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic on the 30th of June, 1993, and he brings them into connection with an order issued by Mr. Petkovic about raising combat readiness to a higher level, which is P3082 and orders under P3128 and P3012. Contrary to the assertion by the Prosecution that that was a case of some sort of subordination, the Defence points out that the only common reference for this -- for -- for the issuing of those documents was the BiH Army attack against the HVO on the 30th of June, 1993. If we follow the chronology, the first thing that happened was the issuing of the order P3019, then P3082, and finally the order co-signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic, P3128. The Petkovic Defence, in paragraphs 253 through 254, states that Mr. Petkovic, on the 30th of June, 1993, after the order P3019 was issued, informed Mr. Bruno Stojic that in all the units measures have been taken to remove Muslims from the HVO units, and that the same was repeated on the 22nd of July, 1993, in his report two days before he left his position as the Chief of Staff. These reports clearly states that measures had been taken in order to disarm Muslim members of the HVO and that additional mobilisation campaign had been carried out. Documents were offered to corroborate this claim. They were 4D480 and P3642. We have to emphasise that it is correct that these documents do not mention that Muslim members of the HVO should be isolated. Those two documents were not presented to Mr. Stojic, because he was in Mr. Petkovic's chain of command, which is proven and corroborated by document P3029, which was delivered to Mr. Blaskic, and the document is identical to 4D48Z. Document P3640 is a six-month report. Mr. Bruno Stojic's Defence points out that the Prosecutor, himself, in his closing argument admitted that on the 30th of June, 1993, the situation changed in the HZ-HB and that that was the date when the war started between the ABiH and the HVO. This is what the Defence claims. And we also claim that the war started with the ABiH attack on the HVO. And now we are moving to the Prosecutor's final brief, to its part entitled as follows: "Stojic had full authority and responsibility for the Defence Department in the HVO." This is not true. Bruno Stojic did not have full authority and responsibility for all the activities of the Defence Department, which we corroborated in paragraph 3 of our final brief. Bruno Stojic did not issue orders to the assistants in the Defence Department, and he also did not issue orders to the commanders of the Main Staff. In paragraph 542, the Prosecutor develops his case and says that Bruno Stojic had wide authorities in managing and controlling the Defence Department, which included issuing order to the assistants of the HVO Main Staff and other bodies. To corroborate his words, the Prosecutor does not proffer a single piece of evidence that would confirm this. Among the documents proffered by the Prosecutor, there's also document P5259. We emphasise that these are the instructions for the work of the SIS in Travnik. This document was not drafted or issued by Bruno Stojic. The document is not signed. The author is not mentioned. However, the heading shows that the document was issued by the security sector and not Bruno Stojic. In paragraph 543, the Prosecutor claims that the collegium of the Defence Department advised Stojic about various defence and military issues and that Stojic put a lot of weight to these meetings and that he told General Praljak that he should personally attend the meeting on the 2nd of September, 1993. General Praljak, however, sent his deputy to that meeting. In footnote 1272, the Prosecutor refers to the testimony provided by Slobodan Bozic, who -- when they claim that the collegium advised Stojic on different defence and military issues. The witness never said that. I'm going to quote the witness: "The collegium was an informal body which was not envisaged by any document. The purpose of the meetings of that body was to discuss all relevant issues, issues of some interest for the Defence Department and the preparation of various documents that were supposed to be adopted at the HZ-HB level or at the level of the president of the HZ-HB. So all those should be discussed, and all members of the collegium could participate, all with a view to finding the best possible proposals and solutions that would be later on referred for further processing." Collegium meetings were not intended to -- to provide advice to Bruno Stojic on Defence and military issues. Many administrative and technical issues of some relevance for the functioning of the Defence Department were discussed at the collegium meetings, and this can be seen in all the transcripts. The transcripts clearly show that every sector was independent in the discharge of their duties and that the head of the Defence Department did not have a say in that. Your Honours, I would like to move on to the topic of the collegium. I would like to show some transcripts. I would not like to be interrupted after showing the first in the series of documents that I intend to show, so I would kindly ask you to call the first break at this moment.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just about time to have the break. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Nozica, please proceed. I was told by the Court Deputy that you had so far used 2 hours and 57 minutes. In other words, there is still -- you have nearly two hours left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information, Your Honour. I will try to finish by the end of this session, and then the final arguments will be presented by my learned friend. Before I continue, I would like to correct the transcript and thank Ms. Alaburic, who -- who pointed this out. On page 19, line 3, I said "lower-ranking commanders," whereas it should be "higher-ranking commanders." I also apologise to the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom for any possible errors regarding numbers, but in the afternoon we will review the transcript, and, in case of need, tomorrow morning correct the transcript before we proceed, or possibly file a motion. Let me now return to the matter of the collegium of the Department of Defence. I will mention everything relevant. I've already pointed out that the collegium discussed administrative matters. The relevant documents in chronological order are 2D1362. That's an invitation to a meeting. Then 2D1363. And I would like to point out that in these minutes, under item 6, it is clear what administrative role Bruno Stojic had in appointing persons, appointing either personnel in individual sectors or in units. Mr. Stojic asked all his assistants to submit proposals for personnel appointments by Monday, 30 November 1992. He also requested proposals for personnel to be appointed to establish certain brigades. The following collegium meeting is 2D1443, and then 2D1444, followed by P880, P1075, and P4646. P4756 is that meeting to which Bruno Stojic invited General Slobodan Praljak, but he didn't come. In his stead, General Matic was there. He was de facto the fourth most important man in the Main Staff. We can see from a discussion in item 1, and the Trial Chamber has the document, that the restructuring of the Main Staff was on the agenda, and this is a matter normally dealt with by the head of the Department of Defence. On 18 September 1992, the head of the Department of Defence did adopt an interim structure of the Main Staff, that is P502, in which the highest ranking positions of the Main Staff were the Chief of Main Staff, the deputy chief, and the assistant chief. As we see from the discussion by General Matic in these minutes, there were dilemmas due to the introduction of new positions, namely the deputy chief and the assistant Chief of the Main Staff, which were absent from the interim structure. So it wasn't clear what the authority of the Chief of Main Staff or his deputy, respectively, were. The highest-ranking person in the Main Staff should have attended the meeting, but he didn't come, and General Matic didn't have the power to take such decisions. Nothing was done, but a new deadline was given to the services of the Main Staff to draft an instruction about the work of the Main Staff. However, this job was never done before Bruno Stojic left the position of the head of the Department of Defence on 10 November 1993. All this is not so important were it not for the insistence of the Prosecution on the fact that Bruno Stojic invited General Praljak. But General Praljak was the highest-ranking man in the Main Staff, and it was normal for him to give his opinion about these matters. Let me now pass to paragraph 545 of the Prosecution final brief where the Prosecution asserts that Bruno Stojic had powers over the armed forces, including the right to issue orders to the Chief of the Main Staff, but he don't corroborate this assertion by any evidence. And that is not surprising, because there is no evidence to corroborate it, and this is a false assertion. The only orders Bruno Stojic ever issued to the Main Staff refer to administrative matters regarding the structure of units which were part of his remit according to Article 9 of the decision on the elements of the structure of the Department of Defence. Furthermore, it is asserted that Bruno Stojic was in a position to order the establishment of HVO units or their merging or splitting. The Prosecution offer Exhibit P3149 to corroborate that, because that document is an order to re-establish the Knez Domagoj Brigade, but this order was not passed by Bruno Stojic. This order was co-signed by the Chief of Main Staff. If this was expressly within his remit, he would have issued the order himself. In item 2 of this order, which is actually within his remit and that's why he co-signs, he gives out a task to the Department of Defence from the remit of the civil sector of the Department of Defence. So this wasn't an order of the head of the Department of Defence, which is confirmed by Exhibit P3151, which is an order issued by Mr. Obradovic, who passes -- passed it on to subordinate units, and in the preamble to that order, he refers to the order issued by the Main Staff rather than the order of the chief of the Department of Defence. Let me move on to the heading in the Prosecution brief that Stojic played an active role in the command and control of the armed forces of the HVO. But Bruno Stojic did not have the authority to command the HVO, nor did he ever do that. This is explained in detail in paragraph 331 of our final brief. Two commanders of the Main Staff have been heard in this courtroom, Milivoj Petkovic and Slobodan Praljak. Both confirmed that they never received an order from Bruno Stojic about the operative commanding of the HVO. The transcript pages where this can be found are 43446 and the following. Also page 50349. The Prosecutor actually confirms that, too, in the first sentence of paragraph 547. No one document used by the Prosecutor to corroborate this claim actually confirms it. The claim of the Prosecution is that Stojic actually commanded indirectly, but that doesn't make sense, because the only way you can command is directly, and the Prosecution's duty was to offer evidence to that effect. In Annex N, the Prosecution lists several documents which allegedly show that Bruno Stojic commanded HVO units. Not one of these documents actually confirms that. I would like to point out the testimonies of the commander of the Main Staff again, which clearly show that Bruno Stojic did not command HVO units in an operative manner. The Stojic Defence does not deny that the Main Staff was under the Department of Defence. The Department of Defence did have authority with regard to the Main Staff as outlined in Article 9. We have said that several times. But the -- but a close reading of that paragraph clearly shows that Bruno Stojic didn't have the authority to either plan or command. Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the possibility that in Annex N of the Prosecution final brief, you may be able to find Mr. Siljeg's reports, who submitted -- which he submitted to Bruno Stojic and other persons. But for the Trial Chamber to decide whether Bruno Stojic received these reports only for his information or to act upon, it is necessary to see that Bruno Stojic did not report -- receive sitreps from commanders of other operative zones. For him to be able to take part in planning or issue orders, even indirectly, as asserted by the Prosecution, then he would have had to have reports from all operative zones, but that is not the case. Therefore, the only conclusion to be drawn is that Colonel Siljeg, in accordance with some procedures that he obviously learned, sent reports both to the Department of Defence and other bodies of the HZ-HB, but there is no evidence that Bruno Stojic ever replied to him with regard to inquiries in these documents or that he gave him instructions or orders. Paragraph 549: Here the Prosecution claims that Bruno Stojic had close and direct connection with Gojko Susak, the Croatian minister of defence, about military matters, and as evidence they offer the transcript from the meeting of the People's Defence Council of Croatia of 3 November 1992, where Susak put forward the information that on 19 August 1992, he had a meeting with 17 officials from Bosnia-Herzegovina, among whom there was Bruno Stojic. This clearly does not corroborate the Prosecution's claim about the existence of direct and close links between Bruno Stojic and Gojko Susak. The Prosecution go on to assert that it is obvious from the transcript of 27 January 1993, that Stojic thoroughly informed Gojko Susak about military operations in Central Bosnia, including Gornji Vakuf, and for that they offer Exhibit P1325 as corroborating evidence. Your Honours, I kindly ask you to review this transcript, because we submit that it does not contain what the Prosecution asserts. The Prosecution further claim that Stojic controlled HVO labour, logistics, and finance. In paragraph 556, the Prosecutor asserts that Witness Miroslav Rupcic confirmed in his testimony that Stojic requested the minister of defence of Croatia to pay for the armed forces and that Susak approved that, but the witness didn't say that. The Prosecutor showed the witness two documents P10290 and 10291. The witness said these documents did not bear Bruno Stojic's signature. This unambiguous statement of the witness is mentioned on page 23375 of the transcript, lines 9 and 10. It suffices to look at these documents to find out that they do not have the letterhead of the Department of Defence. They have no registration number of the Department of Defence or its seal, and they are not signed by Bruno Stojic. During his cross-examination, the witness was shown the settling of accounts of the Department of Defence for 1993. That's P8118, pages 7 and 8. It's a lengthy document. The Trial Chamber has -- has it in its possession. And the overall revenue of the Department of Defence is stated in Croatian dinars. Here the amount is shown which the Department of Defence received from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Department of Finance of the HR HB. The amount received from the Department of Defence of the Republic of Croatia is 16.764.924.236 Croatian dinars. During the witness's testimony of Witness Miroslav Rupcic, a conversion of Croatian dinars into German marks was made which can be found in paragraph 214 of our final brief. The witness testified that toward the end of 1993, that amount equalled 4.488.445 German marks. The reference can be found in transcript pages 23573 and the following. When we presented this document to the witness, Judge Antonetti, based on the information from that document, said that this amount was received from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia is lesser than 10 per cent, which is completely correct. And the transcript -- the relevant transcript page is 23576 through 23571. I apologise. I misspoke. It's transcript pages 23576, line 17 -- lines 17 and 28. Bruno Stojic's Defence points out, and that can also be seen in the documents P1020 and 1291, that the monies were borrowed from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. And the Defence also points out that the monies loaned to the Defence Ministry were raised by the citizens who originated from Bosnia and Herzegovina and who lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina and elsewhere, all over the world, and that was confirmed by the Prosecutor's witness Mr. Rupcic on pages 23579 through 23581 and 23585. We would like to draw your attention, Your Honours, that on that occasion the witness was also shown document 2D532, which was admitted into evidence as 1D1755. The witness explained why those monies were paid into accounts in Croatia rather than in accounts in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It should be pointed out because of the Prosecutor's allegation about the -- about the JCE in this part that concerns financial support to -- provided by the Republic of Croatia that the Defence has presented to the Trial Chamber Exhibit 2D545, which is the guarantee of the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Croatia, dated 13 May 1992. And this guarantee showed -- shows that it was guaranteed to the Crisis Staff of the Muslims of Croatia an amount of $30 million US worth of goods will be delivered as assistance to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, it really is not necessary to provide any comments about these two amounts, because they clearly show that the Republic of Croatia has given ample money, both to the HZ-HB and also provided guarantees to the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that there would be at least a nine times higher amount forthcoming in order to assist the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Paragraph 558: The Prosecution further claims that Bruno Stojic organised special centres, intelligence centres, in Mostar and Zagreb, and he proffers Exhibit P2044. The claim does not arise from that document. The intelligence centre in Mostar had existed even before the war and continued existing during the war. This is corroborated by P7344, pages 41 through 45, where we can see what the role of that centre was -- or, rather, of these centres. These centres were primarily intended for alerting and informing citizens about possible attacks, informing citizens about the passability of different roads, the supply of water, and also they were intended to make a note of all those events. Bosnia-Herzegovina borders on Croatia, and it was only normal for the two centres to co-operate as they do in peacetime. Intelligence centres of that type co-operate during peacetime and during wartime, and they share information of some relevance for each other. In this paragraph, the Prosecutor claims that Bruno Stojic co-operated with the Serbs when it comes to the procurement of weapons from the Serb side. When it comes to the parts of Mladic's diaries and co-operation with the Serbs, we provided a detailed explanation in our final brief, in paragraph 259 -- 252. Bruno Stojic's Defence claims that the purchase of weapons from Bosnian Serbs was the product of the environment in the area of the UHZHB which were under constant attack on the part of the ABiH. They were not in a position to procure weapons in any other way. They were not able to get medical treatment in those enclaves because they didn't have any hospitals. This is confirmed by the Prosecutor's witness EA. The fact that those areas were encircled was used by the Bosnian Serbs as testified by EA to sell their weapons and materiel and technical equipment at prices up to ten times higher than was their real market value. During the examination of that witness, I used the word "blackmail," and indeed it was a blackmail, and Witness EA confirmed that on pages 24904 to 24903 through 24917. The page numbers are 24904, 24913 to 24917. This is also confirmed by document P9967. The document shows the prices which were paid for materiel and technical equipment. Would I like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the fact that the witness was examined and shown this document during his examination, and we also showed him 2D577. In this document, we see the prices that the ABiH paid for the materiel and technical equipment purchased from the HVO and from the arms factory in Travnik. We compared those prices with the witness, and we established that the prices they paid to the Serbs were up to nine times higher. This was recorded on transcript pages 24913 through 24917. We would like to briefly draw the Trial Chamber's attention to document P9965, specifically to the last sentence in that document which shows that the HVO Kiseljak paid 1 million Deutschmarks to the Serbs from their own funds. This is yet another piece of evidence that the local authorities financed the troops in their own areas. I'm now moving on to the part where it says that Bruno Stojic exerted control over the HVO military police. In paragraph 561, there is a description of the administrative activities which were within the remit of Bruno Stojic, as well as of the chief of the military police, Valentin Coric. In paragraph 564, the Prosecutor alleges that one day before the HVO ultimatum, on the 15th of April, 1993, according to the Prosecutor, the ultimatum was on the 15th of April, 1993, so one day before that, the military police commander Lovric issued a plan for the intensive control of the city of Mostar pursuant to an order issued by the Defence Department head, and he mentions document number P1868. However, the Prosecutor's allegation is not correct. This is indeed a plan of the increased control of the city of Mostar. However, the document says that it was being issued because of the complicated security situation as a result of the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO in Konjic. This plan has nothing whatsoever to do with any ultimatum. Witness Dragan Juric testified about this attack by the ABiH, and would I kindly ask you to look at two documents, P1874 and P1879, which illustrate this claim. The same paragraph says that after the BH Army took the North Camp in Mostar, Bruno Stojic subordinated the civilian police, which had manned the front lines, to the commander of the military police. In the footnote, there is a reference to document P3124. However, Your Honours, this is not correct, and you've -- you will see that confirmed in documents P3027 and P3123. These -- these are orders issued by the head of the department of the interior who had the right to command the civilian police. As far as moving the military police from Livno and their arrival in Mostar, the commander of that unit testified, and that testimony was recorded on transcript page 50973, and in his testimony he said whose orders he followed when he did that. In paragraph 567, the Prosecutor claims that -- that after tensions in Prozor in October, Stojic's Defence Department stepped up the HVO control in Mostar by way of issuing an order to the military police through Valentin Coric. The Prosecutor claims that the order was for the military police to get hold of the most important facilities in town. In order to corroborate that claim, they proffered document P619. In this report, it is stated that pursuant to the order of the head of the department, pursuant to a decision of the president of the HVO, certain facilities in Mostar had indeed been taken. A Prosecutor -- Prosecutor's witness, Witness CV, testified and said that this was done in a joint operation of the ABiH and the HVO, and you will see that at -- in the transcript on page 12590, lines 13 through 20. And this was additionally confirmed by Witness Vidovic, and that was recorded on transcript pages 5149 through 51554. In paragraph 568, the Prosecutor offers document P670 to illustrate his claim that that document demonstrates an active role of Bruno Stojic in the military operations in Prozor. The document itself shows that there was a joint attempt by Bruno Stojic and Slobodan Praljak to resolve problems that had arisen with regard to the departure of a group of soldiers from Jajce, Jajce that had came -- come under a Serb attack only one day after the alleged agreement with the H -- with the Serbs, and that took place in Jajce, on the 26th of October, 1992, and this is corroborated by P11380. The document shows that for 40 -- 58 hours there had been attempts to allow an HVO formation to head for Jajce, but there have been attempts to prevent that by the Muslims: "You should try to settle this situation with Muslims in Travnik and Jajce, and you should exert your influence over the Muslims and ensure an unhindered passage towards Jajce on their part." And I end this quote. Why was this quote important, Your Honours? It is important because this unit that headed towards Jajce did that on account of a fierce attack by the Serbs. Jajce was being defended by both Muslims and Croats, and that particular unit was also composed of both Croats and Muslims which is corroborated by document number 3D484. Certainly this document cannot be interpreted as an order, but, rather, as an appeal to do anything possible to save Jajce, which was being defended by both the HVO and the ABiH. The following document that the Prosecution used in order to corroborate his claim that Bruno Stojic had been involved in the events and developments in Prozor in 1992 is P799. The Prosecutor claims that Bruno Stojic called the HVO brigade commander and the commander -- I apologise, Your Honours. I was just checking the time, and I apologise for that. The Prosecutor claims that Bruno Stojic, on the 25th of October, 1992, called the HVO brigade commanders and the commander of the military police in Mostar and invited them to report to him about the situation in Prozor and proffers document P7992 to corroborate that. When we look at the document, we see that this is an invitation to a meeting. However, the conclusion drawn by the Prosecutor certainly cannot be drawn on the basis of this document. The reason why Bruno Stojic sent this invitation is obvious if we look at document P835. Bruno Stojic, only five days after that meeting, issued an order about appointments in the Rama Brigade of other officers and deputy commanders pursuant to the authorities within his remit, pursuant to Article 34 of the Decree on Armed Forces. When we look at these two documents, we can conclude that that was the main topic on the agenda of that meeting. It would not be logical for a Defence Department head to call all the leading officers to travel across the territory to inform him about certain developments seven days post facto. On several occasions, the Prosecutor used documents issued by the assistant for the SIS to the respective units in order to prove some of his allegations, although those documents were never submitted to Bruno Stojic. Bruno Stojic was not in a position to know about the contents of those documents even if they had been sent to the SIS administration. The Prosecutor never proved that Bruno Stojic had full and complete control over a single sector in the Defence Department. Paragraph 571: With regard to the claims in this paragraph of the Prosecution, the Defence points out that there is no evidence showing that Bruno Stojic was aware of the alleged attacks of the HVO after 15 April 1993 in Central Bosnia. And no one document the Prosecution uses to substantiate their claim actually shows that. In paragraphs 572 and 573, the Prosecution claims that the HVO operation against Sovici and Doljani was a large-scale operation that included two operative zones and that it could only be co-ordinated by high authorities, including Bruno Stojic. They likewise claim that the operation was carried out in accordance with the plan, so even if Stojic was not involved, he was at least familiar with the plan. The Prosecution failed to prove any of these claims beyond reasonable doubt. As evidence they offered two orders issued by Miljenko Lasic, but they were not forwarded to Bruno Stojic; as well as document P1915, which shows that it refers to the BH Army attacks on the Herceg Stjepan HVO Brigade in Konjic on 14 April 1993 but which Witness Dragan Juric testified on transcript pages 39318 through 39321. Furthermore, document P2085 wasn't received by either Stojic or the Department of Defence, which can be seen from the log-book of coded messages of the Main Staff, which is P463. The Prosecution also did not prove who this man Dragan is. In paragraphs 574 and 575, the Prosecution claims that Bruno Stojic played a leading role in the military operations of the HVO on 9 May 1993, and substantiates that with BBC footage of 10 May, which the Prosecutor presented in his final arguments. Your Honours will remember that this is Exhibit P4238. I would especially like to point out for the Trial Chamber the words the Prosecution uses -- or, the Prosecution mentions in paragraph 577 are not the words of Bruno Stojic but the words of the journalist. The journalist provides an alleged answer in part of that footage, the alleged answer of Bruno Stojic. But after that, we heard Bruno Stojic's voice. We submit that the words cited were not uttered by Bruno Stojic, because if he had, the journalist would have noted that as he has noted or recorded the -- that part of his statement which is not contentious. There were also valuable observations and questions by Judge Antonetti about this footage and about the way of the office of Bruno Stojic looked as well as the maps in front of him. The transcript pages are 35985 through 35961. About paragraph 579, about shelling Mostar after 9 May 1993 and the alleged reasons for that, the Prosecution claims that Bruno Stojic knows about that based on the testimony of Witness CB. The Prosecution haven't proffered any evidence to support the claim that Bruno Stojic was aware of this statement even if -- if the -- and the Defence asserts that this is wrong and that the witness made it up. This statement was not recorded in any report of the SpaBat. Slobodan Bozic -- we cannot trust a witness who says that he didn't know who Slobodan Bozic was, who regularly contacted the SpaBat as a member of the HVO HZ-HB commission for liaison with international organisations. Now, about paragraph 580 that Bruno Stojic knew about sniping and about the death of Lieutenant Fernandez by a bullet fired by the HVO. The evidence of the death of Lieutenant Fernandez has been analysed. Document 2D117 is a report about the findings of the commission whose task it was to investigate the circumstances of the killing of this lieutenant. This report is dated 14 June 1993, and the allegations from this report were used in the letter that Bruno Stojic sent to the Spanish minister of defence. We would like to remind you that Spanish officers, namely Colonel Castro and Colonel De Salas, also took part in the work of the commission, which means that Bruno Stojic did not put himself in the position to be responsible for the death of HVO soldiers. And we see from report 2D117 that a story was compiled which originates from high officials in Spain, probably by mediation of information from the SpaBat that HVO is to blame and that sanctions are to be taken against the HVO in Croatia. This is the reason why Bruno Stojic wrote this letter to the Spanish minister. So Bruno Stojic didn't put himself in the position to be responsibility for the killing of the HVO soldier as the Prosecution claims. Furthermore, we see that the HVO was not responsible for the death of Lieutenant Fernandez nor has anybody ever established anything else about this event. After the report of this commission, UNCIVPOL got the mandate to investigate the circumstances of the killing of this lieutenant, but they never did that. The document is 2D118. So the Prosecution's claim that the HVO was pronounced guilty of this murder is wrong. I'll get back to the last sentence from report 2D117, because it shows the manipulation of information about the death of Lieutenant Fernandez to the detriment of HVO. This can also be seen from the report by General Petkovic, which is P2808. This manipulation was continued by Witness van der Grinten in his statement given to this Tribunal when he said that Bruno Stojic, when talking to this witness on 16 June 1993, said that he had HVO snipers under his control. In the report from this meeting, which is P286 -- I'm not sure whether this is actually the right document number. I will check it and correct it subsequently, if necessary. Anyway, this document states that the HVO had snipers under their control. This is obviously false testimony, because it is not at all logical that this wouldn't have been mentioned in the report I mentioned if Bruno Stojic had ever said that. But we can see that not even the Prosecutor believe him fully because if we read the last sentence in paragraph 589 of the Prosecution final brief. In paragraph 588, the Prosecution claims that the HVO attacked the BH Army on 24 August 1993, at the North Camp, the hydro power plant dam and the Rastane village. But the Defence states that the footnotes of 1369, 1370 and 1371 of the documents cited by the Prosecution show that it was actually the BH Army who started the attack. And the documents mentioned here were not received by Bruno Stojic. They show who was in a position to decide which HVO unit would be involved in these military operations, but Bruno Stojic took no part in that. Documents P4401 and P4435 about the professional units and their training allegedly contain Bruno Stojic's statements, but these reports do not state when he allegedly said that, and since the BH Army attacked the HVO on the 24th of August, 1993, Bruno Stojic, even if this were correct, couldn't know that this military operation would be launched or who would take part in it. We would like to add that even in the log-book of activities of the SpaBat, which is P1717, and the following period, no conversation with Bruno Stojic is recorded. Paragraph 589: Here the Prosecution asserts that after the BH Army had taken Rastane on 20 September 1993, Stojic and Praljak reacted fast by mobilising all human resources to destroy MOS terrorist groups which had infiltrated the area. They refer to documents P5235 and P5232. These two orders have nothing to do with the HVO operation at Rastane, which is north of Mostar. The evidence we offer is document P9276, which is map 18, which the Trial Chamber can use to see where Rastane is. The BH Army took Rastane on 21 September 1993, which follows from the report of the Main Staff, which is document 2D338. The HVO operations were commanded by the commander of the zone of operations South-East Herzegovina, Miljenko Lasic, which is -- which can be seen in document P5303. The commands of Bruno Stojic -- or, rather, the orders of Bruno Stojic and Slobodan Praljak refer to terrorist groups in the area of Capljina, Capljina, which is south of Mostar, and not Rastane, which is north of Mostar. Slobodan Praljak in his testimony explained that he received an order from Bruno Stojic and that he crossed out "Mostar" from this order and entered "Ljubuski" and added his initial to confirm the changes. The transcript page is T42078, lines 36 -- line 36 through 42082, line 25. These orders show that the task was to mobilise men which was within Stojic's remit but also that the forces gathered should be put at the disposal of Colonel Obradovic. The mobilisation was to be carried out by the military police and the civilian police. That's why the head of the Department of the Interior was -- or, rather, the head of the Department of the Interior issued an identical order, this is 2D3002. This is obviously an urgent intervention, and that's why all three orders are almost identical, except for this essential detail in which the order of Slobodan Praljak differs. He at the end of his order adds that the commander of the first sector, Colonel Obradovic, shall inform him about its implementation in a regular fashion. So everybody acted within their remit. The order of Bruno Stojic, which is P5232, cannot be considered commanding HVO units as claimed by the Prosecution in Annex N. If there had been terrorist groups in the general area of Capljina -- or that there were terrorist groups can be seen from two SpaBat reports of 12 September and 27 September 1993. The documents are P4971 and P5416. In the former document, it is said on page 5: "The logistical patrol that was returning from supplying food to the front line was ambushed at Stanojevici when six HVO soldiers were killed."
