Your Honours, I can offer a map. It is IC1108. It is not in your binder, but it shows where Stanojevici is. It is in the Capljina municipality. In the second report, on page 5, it is stated that the reconnaissance group, upon the request of the HVO, found five dead bodies at Oplicici, two of which were in uniforms with their hands tied behind their backs, and all five dead bodies had a large hole in the back of their heads. Where Oplicici is, namely at the Dubravska plateau and very near the areas where mobilisation was to be carried out, can be seen in IC0018. These documents clearly show that terrorist groups infiltrated the area and that they executed some people, because that is the proper name for the event due to the state in which the corpses were. The corpses were found by SpaBat and described by them. Furthermore, the Prosecutor asserts that Bruno Stojic commended Tuta and the Convicts Battalion after these operations in September 1993 at Rastane instead of launching an investigation and punishing the perpetrators of crimes. The Defence submits that no crimes were committed in September 1993 at Rastane nor can -- may be found in the indictment. Paragraph 591: In this paragraph, the Prosecutor refers to two documents about the alleged information that Bruno Stojic had about the eviction of people from their apartments and transfer of women and children to the left bank. These are documents P5554 and P5518. None of the documents -- or neither of the two were ever submitted to the HVO HZ-HB or Bruno Stojic. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas commented upon one of those documents. The Prosecutor failed to prove beyond every reasonable doubt that Bruno Stojic had any knowledge about those events. Paragraph 593: In this paragraph the Prosecutor alleges that after the crime in Stupni Do, Bruno Stojic proposed that Bruno [as interpreted] Rajic be promoted into the rank of active colonel; that's according to the Prosecutor. As for the assignment of rank to Ivica Rajic, this was not a promotion as the Prosecutor alleges. This was just a proposal. And this can be seen in document P6328, and this was also explained by Witness EA on pages 24904, lines 1 through 17. The Prosecutor did not prove beyond any reasonable doubt that Bruno Stojic knew or was in a position to know about the responsibility of Ivica Rajic about the crimes in Stupni Do. As we look at all of the documents that have been admitted into evidence in this case, we can see that before the 10th of November, 1993, when Bruno Stojic left the position as the head of the Defence Department, there was no suspicion that Ivica Rajic might be responsible for those crimes. In other words, up to that moment, no single element was proffered or established to prove that Ivica Rajic had ever participated in some illegal actions. Furthermore, the Prosecutor alleges that Ivica Rajic continued to report to Stojic, Praljak, and Petkovic about the Serbian Croatian co-operation even after the crime in Stupni Do. He submitted requests and received replies from Stojic on the following day. This is not true. We have to look at documents P6219, which is Ivica Rajic's request, dated 29 October 1993, and the request is for assisting the population in Vares. And also Bruno Stojic's letter, P6267, which refers to a convoy which was supposed to move from Berkovici via Nevesinje to Konjic. That convoy carried aid to the civilian population and the HVO soldiers which were in the territory of Turije, Zabrdje and the Konjic pocket that we often mentioned in this case and that Witness Dragan Juric testified about. So these two documents are not in a causal relationship. In paragraph 594, there is a reference to the fact that Bruno Stojic was directly responsible for the camps and that he participated actively in the establishment of a system which served to expel a number of Muslim detainees and their families and -- and deported them out of Herceg-Bosna. Bruno Stojic was not responsible for the camps, either directly or in any other way, and we provided ample proof of that in our final brief. The Prosecutor offers a document which refers both to the camps as well as to the deportation of Muslims. The Prosecutor offers document P3573. The document itself refutes the Prosecutor's conclusion about Stojic's direct involvement and responsibility for the camps. This is a record of the HVO HZ-HB meeting which took place on the 28th of July, 1993. This is just one of the sessions that discuss the issue of the camps. Your Honours, I suggest that you look at the document P3560, and this document describes one of those sessions that preceded the session described in P3573, the latter discussed at the request of the municipality of Capljina about the transfer of the detainees and the conditions of their detention. The goal was to improve the conditions of their accommodation. A discussion ensued, and a conclusion followed, and this conclusion sayings this: "Prisoners of war have to be provided with good accommodation, conditions in keeping with the Geneva Conventions." And it is also said that if the current accommodation facilities are not adequate, the president of the administration of general co-ordination will assign new locations and transfer prisoners of war to the new locations. And now most importantly: "The accommodation in new locations will be within the purview of the Defence Department." A work group or a task force of three people was appointed at that session, and these three people were tasked with visiting the municipality of Capljina, establish the status of the camps and make proposals to remedy the situation if, indeed, a remedy was needed. At this session it was stated that only when the locations are found, the Defence Department will be in charge of them, but only those locations met the conditions of the [indiscernible] 929 [as interpreted]. We would like to point out that Capljina and Dretelj centres where prisoners of war were accommodated, as well as people serving prison services, were not established in keeping with this decree. Now let's go back to the session which was held on the 20th of July and that the Prosecutor referred to. The document number is P3573. The task force submitted its report to the participants in the session, and you can see -- you can see that the task force had established that some media reports were incorrect. They visited the area. They provided their opinion. And as for the transit centres and the finding of new locations for the transfer of people from Capljina, this is very important, that's why I will move to that, the international Red Cross and other international organisations will be allowed access to those facilities in order to control the conditions of stay of incarcerated persons. Secondly, an initiative is upheld for the opening of a transit centre in Ljubuski for those people who wanted to leave war stricken areas and leave for the third countries. The UNHCR has been informed about that. Another task force of three people has been assigned in order to see what the possibilities were to accommodate a certain number of incarcerated persons. This is the information that Bruno Stojic received at the session, and the special emphasis was put on the transit centres. It was said at this session that the initiative also involved the participation of the UNHCR. In other words, Bruno Stojic was not involved in any other shape or form in any of the activities that were aimed at expulsion and deportation. We would like to emphasise that both commissions that were supposed to establish what the conditions were and possibly find new locations were composed without the involvement of any member of the HVO HZ-HB. The commission that was established by Bruno Stojic in 1993, pursuant document number P3995, never took off the ground. The document number is P3995. We said that in our final brief, and we repeat it today. As far as the role of SIS in the procedure to exchange prisoners, we would like to point out that document of 6D168 shows that the SIS centre provided their opinion stating that there were no hindrances for people to be released from the central military prison but did not make any decisions about that. Document P4686 shows that this particular person was released pursuant to an approval that was issued by the office for exchanges. Your Honours, although SIS centres were integral parts of the SIS administration and the security sector, the Prosecution did not prove that Bruno Stojic knew or was in a position to know about the activities of the aforementioned centre. In paragraph 597, the Prosecutor claims that on the 27th October 1993, Josip Praljak sent a report to Bruno Stojic about the situation at Heliodrom. And he referred to document P6170. The Defence claims that this letter was never sent to Bruno Stojic. Not only did he not receive it, it was not sent to him. The contents of the document show that the information contained in the document is the information sent by the witness to Mr. Naletilic. And for reasons known only to him, he considered him Mr. Bruno Stojic's advisor and a person higher ranking than Bruno Stojic. The link between him and Naletilic is seen in document P6844, which is a report from the crime police department dated 24 November 1993. Mr. Praljak was interview in respect of an unauthorised delivery of documents from the central military prison at Heliodrom to Naletilic. The witness was examined about that before this Trial Chamber, and we can see it in the transcript on pages 1486 through 14873. Here we can see that His Honour -- His Honour Judge Antonetti was surprised to see how the witness could put a lower-ranking person above a higher-ranking person. Namely, he put Mr. Naletilic above Mr. Stojic, and the witness replied to that that this must have been a typo. It was not a typo. We claim that that letter was not even intended for Bruno Stojic's perusal, and whether it was delivered to Mr. Naletilic or not, we don't know that. Besides, if Bruno Stojic, as the head of the Defence Department, was in charge of the central military prison at Heliodrom as the Prosecutor insists, and if the witness Josip Praljak, who was an employee of that prison addressed him as his superior, how is it then possible to explain that the witness, on the 24th of November, 1993, sent a letter to Bruno Stojic under Exhibit P6848? And that was 14 days after the new composition of the government was made publicly known. And it was known to everybody that Bruno Stojic was not part of that government, as can be seen in P6583, and that was also 14 days after Bruno Stojic stopped working in the Defence Department. We move to chapter 7 where it says that Stojic consciously and significantly contributed to the operation of the HVO camps by illegally arresting people and sending them for forced labour. In paragraph 600, the Prosecutor claims that the Defence Department was completely responsible for the HVO, according to Mr. Petkovic. This is not what Mr. Petkovic said so explicitly, and you can see this on page 50670. Your Honour, Witness Petkovic said, and I paraphrase, that in HZ-HB they had prisons for prisoners of war and incarcerated people. There was a decree issued by Mate Boban, which is P9292. Whether Mr. Petkovic knew which of the centres had been established pursuant to that decree's moot at this point, but what we would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention is the testimony of Mr. Petkovic about prison camps and put that testimony in the context of all the other evidence, and we believe that based on all that, the Trial Chamber will be able to draw a correct conclusion. Furthermore, the Prosecutor in this paragraph of his final brief proffers certain documents that should corroborate his claim that Mr. Stojic was responsible for the camps. We will tackle only some of those documents. Your Honours, sometimes -- or, rather, very often when reading Mr. Scott's final brief and all of the other learned friends from the Prosecution, my feeling was that we did not present our Defence case here, that none of the Defence teams called any of their witnesses. The Prosecutor insists on all the charges in the indictment, and it seems that we were here in vain, that we challenged the Prosecutor's case in vain, that we called our witnesses in vain. My learned friend Mr. Karnavas says that it is understandable the Prosecutor doesn't find Defence witnesses credible. But there are some notorious facts. One of them is when Mr. Stojic left the Defence Department, but the Prosecutor does not believe even that. The Prosecutor witnesses themselves corroborated some of our case, but the Prosecutor chooses to ignore those. One of the documents is P193 about the Dretelj Barracks. I really feel bad for having to repeat certain things five or six times, but I'm forced to do that because the Prosecutor chose to include them in his final brief, and I have to react, and I have to point to certain things. So this document P893 is a decision to give the Dretelj Barracks to the military police for their use. This decision has nothing whatsoever to do with the apprehension of persons after the 30 March 1993. Your Honours went there, visited the barracks. It is one building, and behind it there was the centre in which the detainees were held. This decision was adopted at a collegium meeting, which is P880. This building houses the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the military police. It was badly damaged and renovated, which is confirmed by document 2D518. The construction works finished in early March, and this (redacted) on pages 22431 to 22434. I apologise. I must correct what I said. I haven't noticed that. It is Witness C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I will check. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Sorry for the interruption. We need a redaction to be made, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. Madam Registrar, could you prepare an order for redaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I continue? I really apologise. This really was my mistake. I failed to notice. This was confirmed by Witness C on pages 22431, line 11, through page 22434, line 9. The first persons to be taken into Dretelj prison, rather than to the barracks I mentioned, were brought after 30 June 1993. I would not go back to the story what happened on 30 June 1993, but it is beyond any reasonable doubt that this building was being renovated to become a prison and that it was before the BH Army attack, the consequence of which was the arrest of Muslims who were HVO members. The following document the Prosecution mentioned in this paragraph is P2806. In this report of 16 June 1993, Mr. Stojic mentions 504 prisoners under investigation. It is important to stress that this number -- that Bruno Stojic is not the source of this number, but that the EC monitors got it from the prison warden on 11/6/1993 when they visit the prison. This is mentioned in document P2721. Secondly, Bruno Stojic, at the collegium on 2 September 1993, which is document P4756, said: "We have two military prisons; namely the central military prison, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski." Because he had information that the central military prison, and in Ljubuski, people are held against whom investigations are being conducted or against whom criminal proceedings have been launched, and the investigative judge or the president of the court had full powers over them. Bruno Stojic had no knowledge about possible detainment of prisoners of war after the report dated 31 October 1992, which is P677. Bruno Stojic was not familiar with the systematic use of Muslim detainees for forced labour. The Prosecution claims the contrary, but they do not corroborate it with evidence. The SIS administration reports of 20 September 1993, which is 5222, from the Dretelj prison, and the report dated with the same date from the Gabela prison, which is P5223, are -- were sent to the president of the HZ-HB which can be seen from document 2D926. These two reports came about as the implementation of the conclusions reached at the collegium on 2 September 1993. We have already mentioned that this is Exhibit P4756. These reports were never forwarded to Bruno Stojic, because on 15 September 1993, the president of the HZ-HB issued order P5104 to the effect that in detention centres for prisoners of war in which not all conditions prevail as set out by international law of war and Geneva Conventions, these conditions shall be created immediately. The president of the HZ-HB obliged the Main Staff, in item 8, to familiarise all commands and units with that and provide technical assistance in the implementation. This order was also forwarded to the Department of Defence for information and to Bruno Stojic to act upon. This order has also been -- was also sent to all units, which can be seen in documents P5199, 1D1704 and 2D1319. The Prlic Defence stated twice yesterday that this decision was -- or, rather, that this order was adopted by Mr. Boban pursuant to Article 30, which is very correct. This is Article 30 of the Decree on the Armed Forces, which is P588. We don't understand what the problem is here. And this provision in paragraph 1 provides for Boban's right to issue orders, and the Defence created a whole story out of this Article 30, but what does it actually say? Under paragraph (1), it says: "In carrying out the activities from the remit, the commander of the armed forces passes directives, orders, and other acts. "(2) The supreme commander of the armed forces can delegate the implementation of some of the activities, the command and control of the armed forces to the head of the Department of Defence." So that when the supreme commander in issuing orders refers to Article 30, he actually refers to his powers to issue orders. If he had transferred these powers to anybody else, he would have had to refer to Article 30, paragraph (2), which is not the case here. And not only here. I must say once more for the umpteenth time that there's no such document showing that Mr. Boban ever transferred his powers to command the armed forces to Bruno Stojic. It is important to stress, and I'm returning to the sequence of events in connection with the prison, I must stress that at the meeting of 6 September 1993, which is P4841, there was more discussion about the prisons and the finding of new locations. Some tasks were given to the Department of Defence, and a deadline was set of 15 days. If we look at these minutes, it certainly isn't logical to assume that the Department of Defence should be able to do anything within 15 days, because the entire HVO HZ-HB was unable to do so in the past three months. But regardless of that, this conclusion of the meeting held on 6 September 1993 ceased to be relevant when President Boban passed decision P5104, where he precisely names those charged with implementing his decision. In paragraph 611, the Prosecution claims that Stojic and Coric know -- knew that prisoners were taken out for labour and substantiate that with document P8424. The document was drafted on 12 May 1994; in other words, six months after Bruno Stojic had left the Department of Defence and Valentin Coric was no longer chief of military police. In paragraph 613, we -- we read the Prosecution's allegation that Bruno Stojic received reports about extensive destruction of Muslim property in Prozor. The documents mentioned here are P1315 and P3375. These are reports drafted by Zeljko Siljeg which were forwarded to the Presidency of the HZ-HB and the government of the HVO and the Department of Defence, the Main Staff and the operative zone. These reports were drafted based on the obligation that flows from the joint declaration signed by Boban and Izetbegovic on 27 January 1993 in Geneva, by which they obliged the Main Staffs of the BH Army and the HVO to establish the responsibility for the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO. Based on this declaration, the Chief of the Main Staff, on the same day, issued order P1322, whose item 4 obliges the commanders of the operative zone to immediately establish the causes and investigate the consequences and establish responsibility of the members of HVO units and BH Army units for the conflict. These documents clearly show that the -- the commanders of the operative zones were obliged to establish the responsibility. Bruno Stojic was not obliged, either de jure or de facto, to do that. The Prosecution, at paragraph 619, asserts that the HVO HZ-HB held two meetings about the prevention of crime. These are P2606 and P4276. I stress, Your Honours, that the HVO HZ-HB continuously implemented measures to prevent crime and did everything in their power. I have no more time, because I would like to finish before the break, to mention all these government sessions, but the activities of the HVO HZ-HB certainly be a focus of the attention of the Trial Chamber. I'm sure you will find out, and you will notice. But it is important to stress that the activities of the HVO HZ-HB cannot abolish the -- the duty of the commanders of the HVO units whose subordinates committed crimes, which is provided for by Article 27 of the Decree on District Military Courts, which is P587. In paragraph 625, the Prosecution's claim that Bruno Stojic knew and was informed about deliberate killings and rapes committed by the HVO, but the documents to substantiate that were never received by Bruno Stojic. There is -- among these, there is document P2770. That's an intercepted conversation. It has been mentioned many times here. I needn't explain to the Trial Chamber how things go in the army and the war. One service listens in on the other. There's a lot of propaganda on that, and to what extent all that is accurate is questionable. But the Prosecution never showed that this report was submitted to Bruno Stojic nor that the handwritten name "Bruno" refers to him at all. During the -- the final, the Prosecution has read this [indiscernible] name Keza, and said, "I believe it is Keza." We don't know based on what they believe that. We would like to point out that document P2769 shows what was happening on 4 June 1993 in the Dum neighbourhood. This is a report of the military police which recorded the events, but they do not match of the descriptions from the intercepts. Paragraph 626: I would like to -- I have good news for both the Trial Chamber and myself, I'm drawing to an end. With regard to the events at Rastane of 24 August 1993, the Prosecution asserts that -- that this health care sector got involved after these events, and they referred to document P4653. Based on that, it isn't likely that Bruno Stojic knew about these deaths. The cited document shows that this is the reply of the assistant head of Department of Defence for health care to the oral order of the Chief of the Main Staff, Zarko Tole. Bruno Stojic didn't have to know about this activity of the Department of Health. Such a decision or such -- the -- the Prosecutor didn't show that he had de facto full control over the work of all sectors and the Department of Defence. Especially in war, such full control is impossible. With regard to paragraph 629 through 632, the Stojic Defence points out that Bruno Stojic was not de jure or de facto obliged to investigate crimes committed by individual members of the HVO. According to Article 27 of the Decree on District Military Courts which is P587, this was the duty of unit commanders. Your Honours, thank you very much. I will no longer take the floor. My learned friend Mr. Khan will continue after the break, and I would like to thank you accordingly for the good co-operation we had all these years, and once again I apologise deeply to the interpreters, because I am not happy to learn that in this courtroom, and I see Judge Trechsel nodding in confirmation, that was -- that I was one of the fastest and most difficult speakers, and this is why I apologise to the interpreters and to everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to have our 20-minute break now, and I believe that Mr. Khan is going to take the floor. Well, I have very elaborate calculations by the Court Deputy shows us that he has under 30 minutes, maybe 28 or 29 minutes. Since we're going to resume around 10 to 1.00, you'll be working until 20 past 1.00, and in theory, the Praljak Defence should be starting. It might be for a very short time, but they might be able to start and give us some preliminary remarks. I don't know, because I don't know beforehand what they're going to say. So we're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. The Court Deputy is telling me that you have 24 minutes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. President. If you could just give me a moment while I try to get my LiveNote to work. I'll make do. Mr. President, Your Honours, this, of course, is the final few minutes that we have to ask you to consider the case against Mr. Bruno Stojic and to view it in the light that is most favourable to him, because of course the principle of in dubio pro reo means that in relation to each and every issue where there is doubt, that doubt must fall to the benefit of Mr. Stojic. Now, Your Honours, we did not in our brief address the issue of sentence. It is, of course, extremely difficult for counsel on the one hand to strongly and passionately and with full vigour ask for a client to be acquitted on all counts and in the alternative to say, well, Your Honours, in the event you're not with us, in the event that you feel compelled to enter conviction, a sentence of X amount of years must be imposed. But, Your Honours, that's what the Rules require to be addressed, at least in some general terms on sentence. The overarching requirement of general application to any case, in my respectful submission, by any Judge when tailoring the sentence is to do that. It is to tailor the sentence, to individualise the penalty. But some factors appear to be quite clearly pertinent to the overall assessment of the case of Mr. Stojic. Your Honours, in your first decision on provisional release, noted the fact that despite having indications that he was wanted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Mr. Stojic did not go underground. He did not try to an evade justice, but, rather, he surrendered to the jurisdiction of this Court voluntarily. And, Your Honour, it's very clear from the jurisprudence of this court, for example the Simic case, that voluntary surrender may be a factor to be taken into consideration. Your Honour, Mr. Stojic during his time in court has never boycotted the trial. He has never walked out, never been difficult, always co-operated, in my respectful submission, in an exemplary manner with the authority of Your Honours as Judges appointed by the international community to decide his fate and the merits of the Prosecution's case. And, Your Honour, it's my respectful submission that his conduct in trial is also a relevant factor. Mr. Stojic has also asked that the Bench be thanked very properly discharging your own duties for the humanity that each and every one of you have shown him. The record discloses that in relation to provisional release applications, and in relation to application for release on humanitarian grounds, on many occasions the Prosecution were vigorously opposed, opposed the applications put in and they sought even to appeal decisions of the Trial Chamber. But Your Honours, in discharging your function, showed faith in Mr. Stojic, and it's relevant that on each and every occasion, on each and every occasion that provisional release was granted, the terms of that conditional release were complied with. There's been no breach, no suggestion of witness intimidation, and on every occasion he has surrendered in a way that this court proceedings have not been disrupted in any manner. And, Your Honour, the content of those provisional release applications disclose, in part, what that has meant to Mr. Stojic, his wife and his parents. And in my respectful submission, of course, it was the proper course, because the presumption of liberty is, of course, the corollary, the natural consequence of the presumption of innocence, but he thanks you for that. Your Honour, the Blaskic Appeal Judgement, at paragraph 728, and the Kordic and Cerkez judgement, at paragraph 1053, makes it clear that complying with conditions of release and behaviour at trial may be mitigating factors, as does the Simic case of October 2003, that a lack of previous conviction, previous good character, are factors that may be taken into account. Now, Your Honours, I preferred yesterday very briefly to the evidence of Davor Korac, who was Bruno Stojic's superior in the Ministry of Interior, and the fact that he had good relations with members of all communities, and that was echoed by his friend Tomislav Kresic - I hope I pronounced it correctly this time - in relation to his personal life. This is important in looking at the man, not the rhetoric, not the caricature that's being painted, but the man that has been sitting in your presence for these many years. Your Honour, I also referred to a General Hamid Bahto's evidence and that is evidence must be given in a significant weight. It really must be looked at before almost looking at the Prosecution evidence in neutralising some of the invective, to neutralise some of the preconceptions that the Prosecution, that are in good faith, have constantly sought to push forward as the truth. Matters are never as simple as may first appear, and the search for truth requires often a difficult navigation through competing narratives. And, Your Honours, that's the task that you all have to get to grips with in the months ahead. Now, Your Honour, General Makar can hardly be called a partisan witness. As Judge Antonetti noted very pertinently, he's a Croat, but he is a Croat who is married to a Serb, who fought in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Hardly a more balanced mix one could hope for. And that witness had the courage to come to this court in open session and speak on behalf of Mr. Stojic. Now, Your Honours, it's often difficult for all sides in different conflicts and different cases to get hold of witnesses, but to -- there are peculiar difficulties in Defence cases to get witnesses, to be the voice of an individual that is castigated and that faces terrible accusations, terrible crimes, and to speak up for such a person whilst you are living amongst people who get to hear a one-sided narrative largely, who have strong feelings, is a matter of exceptional courage. And witnesses on all sides, Prosecution and Defence, that have come before the Court in those circumstances are to be applauded, but the evidence of these -- and I mention they're Muslims because that's something the Prosecution pointed out, these two Muslim witnesses of Hamid Bahto, and then I'll come to him, the second Muslim, Nedzad Cengic, are important, and the fact that all three witnesses, including General Makar, were members of the Bosnian Army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is extremely important. Now, Your Honour, General Nedzad Cengic's evidence is relevant not just to the assessment of the man that Bruno Stojic is, which may be relevant for other purposes that I started with, but, Your Honour, he describes a chaotic situation, and he also describes his account that when he met Bruno Stojic, Mr. Stojic wanted to help. He was willing. He was not hostile, but he had difficulties, and so he asked General Cengic to come back the next day. And when he did it seems that help had been provided, because in that location were General Praljak and General Petkovic -- and the request was given. The MTS that was asked for was provided. Now, Your Honour, this evidence is not to be sidelined. It's not of no consequence. It's not irrelevant as the Prosecution would have you to believe. It may be difficult, it may be awkward, it may be inconvenient because it does not fit in with the theory that they are pushing, but, Your Honours, it is certainly not irrelevant. And it was revealing, again in response to a question by the learned President Judge Antonetti, that when that witness under oath was asked, Who was Bruno Stojic's superior, who did you believe to be the person above him? He says, "In my opinion --" and I quote: "In my opinion, while we were waiting, it was Mr. Praljak -- as we were waiting for authorisation, Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic, because they had to wait for some sort of agreement to be reached; and then thirdly, as we would then bide our time to see what happened." And in relation to the assistance given, he says later on that he does not -- he did not view those gentlemen as his enemies, and he gave reasons for that. But, Your Honours, the fact that he viewed General Praljak as a superior is not unimportant, in my respectful submission. In reviewing the totality of this mass of documents, Your Honours should not lose sight of reality that the HVO existed before the Defence Department was established. What happened overnight? Did the previous modus operandi suddenly get erased by some act of amazing subordination to an administrative structure? Does that happen anywhere in the world, or did the way the HVO acted before the creation of the Defence Department continue in very important and material respects? We say it did. And Your Honours will be guided by the evidence, but you, no doubt, would have formed your own impression of the various personalities in this courtroom over the last few years, and any suggestion -- and, Your Honours, with all your experience in all candour have on occasion had to use all of that experience to keep this trial on track in relation to some of the personalities in this courtroom, and the suggestion on a human level that somehow Bruno Stojic, in fact, is the commander, effective commander of people like General Praljak, General Petkovic, and equal to the highly educated Dr. Prlic is really a nonsense. It is a nonsense. If fits the case, it's convenient, but it is not the truth. Your Honours, when I discussed yesterday in brief the MTS provided by Croatia, again it is important, and I will simply ask Your Honours to note paragraph 215 of our final brief. What I didn't mention, and again it's important, is the training provided by the Republic of Croatia, and that's detailed at paragraph 216 and also by the document 3D00299 of the 4th of January, 1993. Now -- and again paragraph 278 of our final brief that the wounded members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina described as the army, taken out of context, different snippets different people said at different times, the army being treated in the same hospitals as other Croats, taken to Split, is not consistent on any fair appraisal of the evidence with the Prosecution's narrative. One simply does not give weapons to one's enemies, train one's enemies, treat one's enemies. The only solution, the only fair conclusion is those people are not the enemy in the manner that the Prosecution allege. Your Honours, my learned leader discussed in brief the points in detail, the ultimatums and the importance of that, and we refer to paragraph 172 of our final brief and the fact also that Witness DE, at transcript 15671 to 2, noted that 11 HVO brigades, 1 HVO battalion were under the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in areas not controlled by the HVO. Well, why? Why? Why give men valuable commodities, arms, to help one's enemies in other areas? Well, the Prosecution can't have it both ways. They say, Well, that's because of the fight against the Serbs. Well, what about this joint agreement in Karadjordjevo and Graz? Why have this fight against the Serbs? What necessitated the fight against the Serbs if there's the joint agreement in the simplistic and fallacious manner put forward by the Prosecution? Why help? Your Honour, the help is given because there was no criminal intent to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina by Bruno Stojic. In the relation to the Greater Croatia case, it is important just to look closely at the footnotes relied upon by the Prosecution. In paragraph 169 of their final brief, they rely upon two documents to support the contention that Croatia was behind it all, the Republic of Croatia. Now, P09839, it's under seal and I won't go into the document, but, Your Honours, look at that. But they also quote Prlic, and Prlic says that the reason they did not take Jablanica and Konjic was because, was because, of pressure from the Croatian government not to take it. And in the following paragraph, 170 of the Prosecution's final brief, P09258, again they rely upon -- yes, P09258, they note that President Tudjman would not allow General Praljak to take East Mostar because of political loss. Now, Your Honours, international diplomacy requires mediators. It requires intervention. It requires assistance. And whatever dreams and scenarios were looked at by President Tudjman as to how the final map would look, and it may well have included every conceivable option, the question is whether or not a criminal intent can be discerned or whether or not there is doubt in relation that massive, broad-brush, simplistic view that we say that it is. There is doubt. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution can't have their cake and eat it. They can't. I use that phrase, because sauce for a goose, sauce for a gander has been overdone. It's too well cooked that source. But, Your Honours, the Prosecution constantly refer to this co-operation between the Serbs and the Croatians. In furtherance of this subtext, this underlying idea that there's a deal, an unsavory, underhand deal between those parties, and they refer in paragraph 277, 281, 285 and 289 of their final brief of various co-operation, including ICRC and others. But, Your Honours, they refer in 871 and 888 to the willingness of the Croats to fight with the Serbs in Zepce. Well, Your Honours, Zepce is not part of the area the Prosecution, themselves, contend to be part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And when this comes to assisting Muslims in that area, they say it's not relevant, because actually that's part of, you know, the big JCE theory. And when it comes to helping the Armija of Bosnia-Herzegovina outside, they say it's not relevant. It's outside their geographic area. Well, what they are alluding to in Zepce is the identical argument; they can't have it both ways. The same applies to arms. Your Honours, is this really a true-track policy that the Prosecution would have you believe, or is such an understanding -- would such an understanding amount to a one-sided appraisal of the evidence? They can't have it both ways. They're trying to have it both ways and it should be rejected. Your Honours, Bruno Stojic never met President Tudjman. Never met him. It can't be glossed over. It can't be ignored. It has significance. Your Honours must decide what is that significance. We say the fact that General Petkovic and Praljak and Dr. Prlic met him reveals who are the most important individuals. Your Honours, the fact that prior to April 1992 Bruno Stojic was the commandant for logistics and in December 1993 he was in production of weapons is important. Are the Prosecution saying that suddenly he was catapulted to high office and high command, operational control or administrative control, standing astride Bosnia -- the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a colossus or is the reality actually that his role was administrative and he did not have effective command and control. Your Honours will see annexed to our final brief a list, a selection of formalising documents, or documents that Bruno Stojic formalised in relation to decisions that had been previously taken by others. Did he have effective command or was he a rubber stamp in those material respects? Your Honours, the Defence say he never had. He was never part -- there wasn't a massive JCE as alleged. He was not part of it. He had no knowledge of it. The Prosecution theory is not supported in important and material particulars. It is our respective submission, Your Honours, not to be swayed by emotion or invective, not by the hard work done by my learned friends opposite or their sincere belief that they have the truth in their hands and all Your Honours need to do is accept it as gospel. Your Honours, we say that there is doubt and that requires but one conclusion that our client is acquitted. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Khan. You were very well within your time limit. Thank you for that. We are going to start with General Praljak's Defence. We still have 30 minutes. Let's try to use them as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, just as you requested from us from preparations for the session, I will inform you that General Praljak's Defence will present its arguments in the following way: I will be the first to speak, and I will respond to the Prosecutor's allegations that in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the critical time there was a state of an international armed conflict in place, and with this regard that Bosnia and Herzegovina was under occupation. After me, my partner Mrs. Pinter will respond to the Prosecutor's allegations from the Prosecutor's brief, mostly from the chapter dealing with the criminal responsibility of Slobodan Praljak, which is chapter 11 in the Prosecutor's brief, and, finally, again in keeping with your decision about the schedule of these proceedings, General Praljak will personally address the Trial Chamber, and he will take the 30 minutes that were given to him. As regards the international armed conflict, the Prosecution claims that in Bosnia and Herzegovina there was a state of -- the state of an international armed conflict between April 1992 to -- and March 1994. The -- this is presented in paragraphs 71 through 92 and connected paragraphs 160 to 106. Let me remind you that even during pre-trial, the Prosecutor claimed that the Republic of Croatia was not the master of the war between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the trial, the Defence adhered to that position and many pieces of evidence were presented to that effect. I'm not going to repeat arguments that corroborate this assertion. My learned friend has just mentioned some of them. I would just like to remind you of a number of facts that point to the fact that it was impossible to believe that the Republic of Croatia was party to an international conflict with Bosnia-Herzegovina, either directly or indirectly, and that it, either directly or indirectly, supported only the HVO. General Praljak will speak about those facts himself. The Republic of Croatia recognised a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately after the latter state proclaimed its independence in April 1992. That was only a day after the recognition by the European Union. Bosnia and Herzegovina then set up its embassy in Zagreb only a few days after the recognition. Diplomatic relations were established, and very importantly never ever during the war from 1991 to 1994, a single government or a single representative of the government of the Republic of Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina stated either implicitly, let alone explicitly, that there were hostilities between the two states. I would like to remind you of the old theory that was abandoned in the international law and that was that a war had -- has to be declared. That theory was abandoned. However, there has to be a display of political will. Something has to be in place. But that didn't happen. Nobody every said, We are in war with the other state. Without any precedence in history, the Republic of Croatia never introduced any restrictive measures with regard to the property or assets of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its citizens in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The Prosecutor simply ignores these and similar facts. It is certain that in the history of international relations and conflicts, there's no such precedent. It never happened anywhere in the world that one of the parties to the conflict, simultaneously while the conflict lasted, helped the other side to the conflict to survive the aggressor. Witness Peter Galbraith, whom I don't quote gladly because his words were totally unacceptable to us, however, despite his political views, mind you, he was not a witness, he was just presenting his political views, however, after all those words, at one point during cross-examination on the 13th of September, 2006, he said, and that was recorded on page 6599, he confirmed that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not have survived without the positive views and assistance coming from the Republic of Croatia. This fact imposes a question: Why would the Republic of Croatia have done all of the above mentioned if there had been a plan in place for the Republic of Croatia to carve up some of the territory and assisted the Croatian Defence Council with a view to achieving that? The Prosecutor offers a very simple and naive answer when the Prosecutor says it's a two-track policy. The Defence replies to that: This is a naive response which ignores facts. Second of all, no concrete piece of evidence was every proffered in order to corroborate the two-track policy theory. Thirdly, every policy, especially international policy and especially in such situations, is, in one way or another, a two-track policy. There is no single state in the world that would have revealed all of its cards under such circumstances. The Prosecution claims that the Republic of Croatia had territorial aspirations and that it wanted to carve up one part of the territory of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, and even in that context it develops a thesis about the existence of an international armed conflict. In addition to the aforementioned facts that clearly show that that was not the case, let's look at the testimony of Miomir Zuzul in the transcript on pages 27644 from line 15 to 27646, line 5. The witness told us in this courtroom that while the peace negotiations were going on, and never stopped, Izetbegovic offered to Tudjman to take one part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The so-called Herzegovinian municipalities are what the Prosecutor refers to as Banovina. Tudjman refused. I would like to mention that to corroborate the fact presented by Miomir Zuzul, the Defence proffered the statement by Jean -- Jacques Klein pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Mr. Klein is an American general who was a high-ranking UN officer in the Republic of Croatia at the critical time. He confirmed Zuzul's words. Unfortunately, and I repeat unfortunately, for reasons still unclear to me, the Trial Chamber did not admit that statement into evidence like so many other documents. It seems that the Trial Chamber in this case does not accept the generally accepted principle, and that is the -- more information and evidence in this case will make it easier to come to the truth. Let's go back to our main topic. If the Republic of Croatia had had any territorial pretensions towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, the aforementioned offered -- offer attested to by Witness Zuzul would have materialised, but it didn't and that's a fact. Why would the Republic of Croatia have actively acted in Bosnia-Herzegovina, allegedly assisting only the HVO in the conflict with the BiH Army if it is true that it could have gained the desired territory through negotiations? The offer was on the table. But the Prosecution doesn't have an answer to that. The Prosecution never even mentioned that in his final brief. They simply refuse to see the fact because they do not fall into place. I hope that the Trial Chamber will see and will recognise even those facts which do not fall into place with the Prosecutor's thesis. There is unequivocal evidence which unambiguously and very clearly point to the fact that the political leadership of the Republic of Croatia not only supported the creation of a new independent State of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also that during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it actively supported the survival of that new independent state. And the facts are as follows: Firstly, the political leadership of the Republic of Croatia, and even the ruling party, the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia, directly called and appealed to the Croatian citizens in Bosnia and Herzegovina to take part in the referendum, to respond to the referendum, and to vote at that referendum for an independent State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me remind you that was an international condition imposed upon the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina if it wanted to be recognised as an independent state. The world told them you have to have a referendum, and they had it. The Croats participated in the referendum and voted in favour. Obviously, the voting process was confidential, and we don't know who voted in what way, but we are aware of the mathematics. The referendum was successful and resulted in the declaration of an independent state in April 1992. In view of the number of constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the number of voters, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, the referendum would not have been successful. It would have fallen through had the Croats not responded to the referendum, and results show that they voted in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. The mathematics are clear here. The Republic of Croatia lobbied and therefore unequivocally supported the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, the Republic of Croatia was in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina on its borders, and it is a fact that simply cannot be ignored. And yet the Prosecution decides to ignore this fact. In the chaotic situation when the SFRY was falling apart, the representatives of municipalities in which Croats were the absolute, or at least relative minority, established the HZ-HB on 18 November 1991 as an interim body to perform all the functions which the then state authorities did not carry out. This created the conditions for the subsequent establishment of the HVO in April 1992 as an executive body and the HVO as a military component necessary to defend BiH against the aggression of the JNA. The HZ-HB or the HVO at that moment were the only, and I repeat, only organised force in BH which, at least to some extent, was able to stand up to the aggression with weapons. It is a notorious fact that both Muslims and Croats voluntarily joined HVO units and defended BH together until the end of 1992, and to some extent until May 1993 when the conflict between them began. Interestingly, though, even then they fought jointly in those areas of BH where there was no direct conflict between the two parties. My learned friend Mr. Khan has just said something about this. If we take into consideration that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared the state of war only on the 20th of June, 1992, the 20th of June, at a time when the JNA had already occupied the greatest part of the territory that it had wanted to occupy, or we could almost say they had taken nearly everything, it is clear that only the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the HVO started to defend the country timely. Perhaps I should cite Exhibit P00274, the Decree on the State of War. The Presidency declared the state of war only on the 20th of June. This corroborates what we have been putting forward, namely that the HZ-HB has been -- or, rather, was established for the very reason because there was nobody else to defend the country. Only on the 20th of June does the Presidency declare the state of war, and of course there is some time necessary to organise, to prepare things so that somebody actually can start fighting the Serbian aggression. The facts I mentioned, especially the referendum on independence and the timely organisation of defence of BH clearly show that the Republic of Croatia wanted an independent State of Bosnia-Herzegovina on its borders and that with that and active participation of the Republic of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina very probably never would have come or survived as an independent state. How is the Prosecution's argument about the existence of a JCE and an international armed conflict compatible given the facts I have just stated? The only possibility to make such assumptions is total ignorance of these facts. Another thing I would like to mention is a technical circumstance, but, still, it's about the time of the commission of the offence. In their final brief, the Prosecution state that the international armed conflict existed in BiH at least until April 1992 until March 1994. In order to establish the facts, we must determine when the alleged international armed conflict actually began and how long it lasted. We need that to assess the evidence the Prosecution mentioned in their Annex C. Of course I can't go into every detail, but I'm only trying to paint rough picture for you to see yourselves. The first nine documents mentioned in Annex C, and these are documents that according to the Prosecution are evidence confirming the existence of an international armed conflict, the first nine of these refer to events before the declaration of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, before 5 April 1992. I can understand these documents only in the following way: Bosnia-Herzegovina was still part of the SFRY, which was breaking apart, and Croatia was already at war with that same country, SFRY, because the Army of SFRY was at the same time attacking Croatia. These documents are totally irrelevant as evidence for the existence of an international armed conflict, because Bosnia-Herzegovina did not yet exist as a country at that time. No one document cited in Annex C was drafted or refers to after the 9th of May, and that's the date which, according to us, can be considered as the earliest date of the start of the conflict between the HVO and the BH Army, but even that document is not a good foundation for the Prosecution's conclusions. The OTP only interprets various documents in such a way, neglecting the context of events and, of course, without taking into consideration those events and all evidence that show that the argument of Croatia as the master of war in BiH is totally irrational. There are many documents in Annex C that refer to HV documents and have to do with the southern front, from Split to Dubrovnik roughly. The Trial Chamber has heard much about this already. The witnesses are mentioned: Beneta, Petkovic, Praljak, Zuzul, and so on. But anyway, the OTP say that the southern front are -- southern front is -- is a part of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is nonsense, because the southern front is a front line in Croatia. And, of course, you cannot wage war without occasionally crossing the border line. The documents cited by the OTP here must be viewed in context with -- with the following documents: 5D64, that's a joint statement of Tudjman and Izetbegovic; then 3D647, that's the agreement on friendship and co-operation from the summer of 1992; then there is 1D02283 of 25 February; then there's the Decree of the Presidency of BH about the armed forces, which is 4D410, and there are similar -- there is similar evidence. Only when you take into consideration all that, you can see that there's undoubtedly a military co-operation and that HV troops are active along the border to protect the -- their own units in Dalmatia. Exhibit 3D450 and 3D420 show that the HVO is one of the two components of the Defence forces of BH. This is a decision of the Presidency of BH on the appointment of the commander of the TO, dated 27 May 1992. It is a fact that that decision does not mention the municipalities that are part of the HZ-HB. So we can conclude from that that Izetbegovic, himself, considers that Defence in these municipalities has been already organised by the HVO, and, thus, he appoints commanders only for those regions of BH in which there is no defence yet. So those people down there are already putting up a defence, but -- and these are -- there is no defence, so we'll appoint commanders. The OTP say that the Croatian control over the HVO can be established based on the fact that Praljak was the commander and had de jure and de facto control over HVO units of the BH Army. In other words, they implied that General Praljak was an agent of the Republic of Croatia. The paragraphs of the Prosecution brief are 71, 75, 76, 673, and others. Your Honours -- or, actually, I can still cover some ground. Two more sentences. The evidence, such as the testimony of General Praljak, the testimonies of other witnesses and documents, clearly show that General Praljak had different statuses at different points in time during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but he was always a volunteer in various roles though. He was a common soldier. He was a -- he was commander of a small area in early 1992. He was a mediator in a peace mission, and he was also commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. These are more or less undisputed facts. What is not undisputed, though, is that General Praljak had de facto and de jure control. I think that this is a convenient moment for me to stop before moving on to another topic. Your Honours, if I may, tomorrow, according to our math but, actually, of course, you are the time -- the main time-keeper, if I may compliment you in this manner, we need -- we will be about 15 minutes short, and I mean the Praljak Defence, for all of us to say what we have. So if we could be accorded 15 minutes more tomorrow, and we can finish, because, to my mind, I think we are some 15 minutes short. That is, we will be able to squeeze into five hours. So perhaps we could sit for 15 minutes longer. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The Legal Officer can liaise with the Legal Officer in the Tolimir case, because one of the Judges sitting here also sits in that case.
